passage:
Monday: Zubair knocked down Rudra's block tower and ran off laughing. Rudra cried.
Wednesday: It happened again. This time Tanuja Ma'am crouched down beside Zubair. "Look at Rudra's face. It's wet. His mouth is turned down. He's sad." Zubair looked. He stopped smiling.
Friday: Zubair bumped Rudra's tower by mistake. He stood still, looked at Rudra's face, and said, "Rudra sad?" Then he picked up a block and held it out to him.

qa.q: What did Zubair do on Monday?
qa.a: He knocked down Rudra's block tower and ran off laughing.

qa.q: What does Zubair stopping smiling on Wednesday suggest?
qa.a: It suggests he was no longer amused and was starting to feel for Rudra, connecting Rudra's wet, sad face with what he had done.

qa.q: What did Tanuja Ma'am's approach add that scolding would not?
qa.a: By crouching and pointing to Rudra's wet face and turned-down mouth, she helped Zubair see the feeling, which builds empathy.

qa.q: How might Rudra feel when Zubair holds out a block on Friday?
qa.a: Rudra may feel noticed and comforted, seeing that Zubair cares that Rudra is sad. 🙂

grounding: Shows a teacher crouching to point out a friend's visible sadness so a young boy links his action to the tears, and empathy grows.

passage: It was raining, so all twenty-five children were stuck indoors, and lunch was in five minutes. In the noise, Sachin snatched the green crayon from Ayaan, and Ayaan began to cry. Chandrika Miss had a stack of plates in her hands. She put them down anyway and crouched to Sachin's height. "Sachin, look. See Ayaan's eyes? They're wet. His face is all crumpled. Ayaan is sad." Sachin looked at Ayaan for a long moment, the crayon still in his fist. His own face went quiet. Slowly, he opened his hand.

qa.q: How many children were stuck indoors?
qa.a: All twenty-five children were stuck indoors.

qa.q: What does Sachin's face going quiet suggest?
qa.a: It suggests he was noticing Ayaan's sadness and starting to feel it himself.

qa.q: Why was it worth Chandrika Miss putting down the plates, even with lunch so close?
qa.a: Taking a moment at Sachin's level to point out Ayaan's wet eyes helped him link the snatch to the tears, which a quick telling-off would miss.

qa.q: What would change if Chandrika Miss had just taken the crayon back herself?
qa.a: Ayaan would have the crayon, but Sachin would miss seeing Ayaan's sadness and learning why his action mattered.

grounding: Shows a teacher, despite a busy rainy day, crouching to show a child his friend's wet eyes so he links his action to the friend's sadness.

passage:
In the colony playground, Francis snatched the ball from Jeevan and ran off laughing. Jeevan sat down in the dust and cried.
Miss Joyce, who ran the evening play group, walked over to Francis and crouched down so their eyes were level.
"Francis, look at Jeevan," she said softly. "Look at his face. It's all wet. He's sad."
Francis looked. Jeevan's cheeks were shiny with tears.
"What happened just before he started crying?" Miss Joyce asked.
Francis looked at the ball in his hands. "I took it," he said, very quietly.

qa.q: Who ran the evening play group?
qa.a: Miss Joyce.

qa.q: What was Francis feeling when he looked at Jeevan's wet face?
qa.a: He began to feel a little sorry and uncertain, realising his grab made Jeevan sad.

qa.q: Why did Miss Joyce's approach work?
qa.a: She crouched down, pointed to what was visible on Jeevan's face and asked what happened, helping Francis link his action to his friend's tears.

qa.q: What is Jeevan experiencing?
qa.a: He feels sad and upset after his ball was taken.

grounding: A teacher crouches down and points to a friend's tears, helping a young child link his grabbing to his friend's sadness.

passage:
"Kalyan, come here, please," said Ganga Ma'am. She knelt down beside him in the block corner.
"I didn't—"
"I'm not cross. Look at Bittu. What do you see?"
Kalyan looked. Bittu was sitting by the tower, which was now on the floor.
"He's crying."
"Yes. His face is wet. His lip is shaking. What happened to his tower?"
"It fell."
"What made it fall?"
Kalyan looked at his foot. "I kicked it."
"So Bittu is sad because the tower he built fell down."
Kalyan was quiet. Then he said, "He's sad."

qa.q: What happened to Bittu's tower?
qa.a: It fell on the floor after Kalyan kicked it.

qa.q: What was Kalyan feeling when Ganga Ma'am called him?
qa.a: He was worried about being in trouble, starting to say "I didn't".

qa.q: What did Ganga Ma'am do that helped Kalyan understand?
qa.a: She knelt beside him, said she wasn't cross, and pointed to Bittu's wet face and shaking lip, helping Kalyan link his kick to Bittu's sadness.

qa.q: What is Bittu experiencing?
qa.a: He feels sad and hurt that his tower was knocked down.

grounding: A teacher kneels beside a child and points to his friend's visible tears, helping him link his action to his friend's sadness.

passage:
Nursery room note, Wednesday

At snack time, Harsha pushed Sachin off the small chair so he could sit by the window. Sachin fell, not hurt, but he cried loudly.
Harsha turned away and started eating his biscuit.
I crouched down next to Harsha. I said, "Look at Sachin. See his face? It's wet. He's sad." Harsha looked. I asked, "What happened to Sachin's chair?" Harsha said, "I pushed." He looked at Sachin for a long time.
Then he held out his biscuit to Sachin. I'll share this with both families at pick-up. 🙂

qa.q: Why did Harsha push Sachin off the chair?
qa.a: So he could sit by the window.

qa.q: What was Harsha feeling when he looked at Sachin for a long time?
qa.a: He seemed to start feeling sorry, as he connected his push with Sachin's crying.

qa.q: What did the writer of the note do that helped?
qa.a: The writer crouched down, pointed out Sachin's wet face, and asked what happened, which helped Harsha link his push to his friend's sadness.

qa.q: What was Sachin experiencing when he fell?
qa.a: He was upset and startled, crying loudly even though he wasn't hurt.

grounding: A nursery note describes an adult crouching down and pointing out a crying child's wet face, helping another child link his push to the tears.

passage:
At the anganwadi in the village, Gopal snatched the mud-brown ball from Sunaina and ran to the neem tree.

Sunaina sat down in the dust and cried.

Anjali Didi, the teacher, walked over and crouched until her eyes were level with Gopal's. She didn't shout.

"Look at Sunaina," she said softly. "See her face? It's wet. Her mouth is turned down."

Gopal looked. He held the ball tighter.

"She was playing with the ball. Then you took it. Now she's crying."

Gopal looked at the ball. Then at Sunaina. His lip wobbled a little.

qa.q: Where did Gopal run with the ball?
qa.a: He ran to the neem tree.

qa.q: What does Gopal's wobbling lip suggest?
qa.a: It suggests he is starting to feel sorry, linking his snatch to Sunaina's sadness.

qa.q: Which choice by Anjali Didi worked, and why?
qa.a: Crouching down and calmly pointing to Sunaina's wet face helped Gopal see how his action made her sad, without shaming him.

qa.q: How does Sunaina feel when the ball is taken?
qa.a: Sunaina feels sad and upset, sitting in the dust crying.

grounding: A teacher crouches and points to a friend's tears so the child can link his action to the other's sadness, building empathy.
